strengths: INTUITOR offers a simple, practical way to train on unlabeled prompts: replace GRPO’s correctness reward with an existing self-certainty metric, without a separate reward model or verifier.

The empirical coverage is substantial, including multiple Qwen sizes through 14B, Llama and OLMo models, and mathematics, coding, knowledge, and instruction-following benchmarks. The larger-model results strengthen the evidence beyond the main small-model experiments.

Several results are promising. For Qwen2.5-3B, INTUITOR improves LiveCodeBench accuracy from 9.3% to 15.3%, versus 8.5% for GRPO. For Qwen2.5-14B, it achieves comparable or better reported results than GRPO across all six benchmarks.
The online-versus-frozen reward comparison, KL ablations, and confidence–correctness analysis provide useful observations about training dynamics and failure modes.
weaknesses: The distinction from closely related confidence and entropy optimization methods is insufficiently established. Self-certainty is borrowed from prior work, and the main algorithmic change is its substitution into GRPO. Appendix A.4 tests entropy minimization only on Qwen2.5-1.5B; moreover, its displayed reward is negative sum p log p, which is positive entropy. Maximizing that expression would encourage entropy maximization. This may be a typographical error, but without clarification and broader matched comparisons, the central comparison against alternative intrinsic rewards is unreliable.

Training specifications contain material contradictions. Section 4 gives learning rates of 3e-5 for MATH and 1e-5 for code, whereas Table 7 gives 3e-6 and 1e-6. The main text specifies a default KL coefficient of 0.005, versus 0.0005 in Table 7; Appendix A.1 specifies 16 completions for larger models, versus 14 in the table. These discrepancies prevent confident reproduction and are especially consequential given the demonstrated KL sensitivity.

The evidence does not cleanly separate improved reasoning from prompt adaptation and output formatting. The base Qwen2.5-1.5B scores only 0.2% on GSM8K under the chat template and initially produces gibberish. Although instruction-tuned models provide some additional support, suitable base-model prompting controls and formatting or self-training baselines are needed to identify what drives the largest gains.

Broad claims of superior transfer and matching supervised RL exceed the consistency of the results. Both small Qwen models trail GRPO on the mathematical benchmarks; the 1.5B model also trails on CRUXEval. Qwen2.5-7B trails GRPO on LiveCodeBench, while OLMo shows essentially no transfer advantage. No repeated training runs or uncertainty estimates establish the reliability of modest differences.

The claim that online self-certainty prevents reward exploitation rests on a short comparison in one setting. Confidence–correctness separation after training does not establish resistance to future exploitation. Likewise, ten examples and selected qualitative traces cannot establish that longer explanations cause better reasoning or reflect improved self-understanding; length-controlled and reasoning-ablation experiments are missing.

The interpretation of self-certainty needs greater care. KL(U||p) can increase because probabilities of unlikely vocabulary items shrink, without implying better task understanding or correctness. The mode-seeking versus mode-covering discussion does not justify the consequences of maximizing this divergence. This matters because the paper’s proposed mechanism relies heavily on interpreting increased confidence as improved reasoning.

strengths: The paper addresses an important question: whether useful reasoning improvements can be obtained without labeled answers or execution-based rewards. INTUITOR is simple to integrate into GRPO and avoids a separately trained reward model.

The reported empirical gains are substantial in several settings. For Qwen2.5-3B, MATH-only training improves LiveCodeBench from 9.3% to 15.3% and CRUXEval-O from 23.6% to 41.6%, exceeding the corresponding GRPO results.

The appendix meaningfully broadens the evaluation beyond small Qwen models to larger Qwen models, Llama, and OLMo. Qwen2.5-14B results are particularly encouraging: INTUITOR matches or exceeds GRPO across all six reported benchmarks.
The online-versus-offline reward comparison, KL ablation, training trajectories, and correctness–confidence analysis provide useful empirical observations beyond final benchmark scores.
weaknesses: The closest baseline comparison has an unresolved mathematical error. Appendix A.4 defines the purported negative-entropy reward as minus the sum of p log p, which is positive entropy. Maximizing this expression encourages entropy maximization. This could be a transcription error, but without implementation evidence the reported collapse cannot establish superiority over entropy minimization. Moreover, this comparison covers only the fragile 1.5B setting, rather than the stronger models where the main comparative claims should also be tested.

Material hyperparameter contradictions undermine reproducibility. Section 4 gives a default KL coefficient of 0.005, whereas Table 7 gives 0.0005; the text gives learning rates of 3e-5 and 1e-5 for math and code, whereas Table 7 gives 3e-6 and 1e-6. Appendix A.1 specifies sixteen sampled responses for larger models, but Table 7 lists fourteen. These discrepancies are consequential because the paper itself demonstrates strong sensitivity to regularization and reports initial collapse when scaling.

The claimed novel RLIF paradigm is insufficiently distinguished from existing intrinsic-reward and self-rewarding approaches. The concrete contribution combines an existing self-certainty metric with standard GRPO. Establishing its specific advantage requires stronger comparisons with the cited entropy/confidence methods; the limited and ambiguously specified entropy experiment does not provide this.

Reasoning improvement is not adequately separated from prompt adaptation, formatting, and additional inference tokens. The 1.5B base model scores only 0.2% on GSM8K under the chosen chat template, and much of the qualitative evidence concerns recovery from invalid outputs. More suitable base-model prompting controls, matched generation budgets, and analysis conditional on valid outputs are needed. Ten questions and selected examples do not establish the proposed mechanism of improved self-understanding.

Several claims exceed the evidence. Online scoring avoids one observed offline exploitation pattern, but this does not demonstrate that it prevents reward hacking generally. Correctness–confidence separation is not a calibration or robustness guarantee. Superior transfer is also inconsistent across settings: 1.5B CRUXEval favors GRPO, 7B LiveCodeBench slightly favors GRPO, and OLMo transfer gains are negligible or negative.

The paper reports no repeated-training variability or confidence intervals for benchmark comparisons. Consequently, small differences cannot support claims of superiority or equivalence. Combined with the unresolved baseline and reproducibility issues, this leaves the contribution below the acceptance threshold despite promising results.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: improving reasoning without task-specific correctness rewards. Using self-certainty as a GRPO reward is simple and potentially broadly useful.
The empirical coverage is substantial, spanning mathematical reasoning, coding, and instruction following across Qwen, Llama, and OLMo models, including models up to 14B parameters.

There are meaningful positive results. For Qwen2.5-3B, INTUITOR improves LiveCodeBench from 9.3% to 15.3%, versus 8.5% for GRPO. For Qwen2.5-14B, it matches or exceeds GRPO across the reported benchmarks without using gold answers for rewards.
Plurality-voting and random-reward baselines, KL ablations, and online-versus-frozen reward experiments provide useful evidence beyond the main performance table.
weaknesses: The comparison with closely related entropy-based methods is insufficient. Appendix A.4 defines its supposedly negative-entropy reward as minus the sum of p log p, which is positive entropy; maximizing the displayed reward would maximize entropy. This may be a typographical error, but it leaves the collapse result difficult to interpret. Testing this baseline only on the repetition-prone 1.5B model also does not establish a general advantage over entropy minimization.

Training details contain material contradictions. Section 4 gives learning rates of 3e-5 for math and 1e-5 for code, whereas Table 7 gives 3e-6 and 1e-6. The default math KL coefficient is 0.005 in the main text but 0.0005 in Table 7, and Appendix A.1 specifies 16 sampled responses while Table 7 lists 14. Figure 2 also depicts a frozen reference scorer despite the emphasis on online policy scoring. These discrepancies impede reproduction.

The distinction between improved reasoning and improved compatibility with chat prompts is unresolved. The Qwen2.5-1.5B base model scores only 0.2% on GSM8K under the chosen template. Appropriate base-model prompting controls, instruction-tuned comparisons, and matched inference-token budgets would help determine how much improvement reflects reasoning rather than formatting or longer answers.

Claims of superior transfer and matching supervised RL need qualification. The smaller INTUITOR models consistently trail GRPO on the math benchmarks; coding advantages become mixed across larger models and architectures. No repeated training seeds or uncertainty estimates establish the reliability of smaller differences, including several instruction-following gains.

The mechanistic and robustness claims exceed the evidence. Ten selected questions and qualitative examples do not establish that longer explanations cause better reasoning. A short online-versus-offline experiment cannot establish that online self-certainty prevents reward exploitation, especially given the behavioral collapse reported when initially scaling the recipe. The mode-seeking/mode-covering discussion also applies terminology associated with KL minimization to an objective that maximizes divergence without adequate justification.

The methodological novelty is narrower than the proposed new-paradigm framing suggests: the method combines an existing self-certainty metric with standard GRPO, alongside acknowledged concurrent intrinsic-reward approaches. The promising empirical contribution warrants attention, but stronger comparisons and resolution of the reproducibility issues are needed to clear the acceptance threshold.

strengths: INTUITOR is simple and potentially useful: it replaces correctness rewards in GRPO with an existing self-certainty metric, requiring neither answer labels nor executable verifiers during training.

The empirical coverage is substantial, including multiple model families, scales up to 14B parameters, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following. The larger-model results strengthen the contribution beyond the initial small-model experiments.
Several improvements are meaningful. Qwen2.5-3B improves LiveCodeBench accuracy from 9.3% to 15.3%, while Qwen2.5-14B reaches 77.0% on MATH500 versus 75.8% for GRPO.

The appendix provides useful investigations of KL regularization, alternative rewards, direct optimization, rollout counts, sequential training, and failure cases. Comparing online and frozen confidence scorers is particularly informative.
weaknesses: The closest reward baseline has an unresolved mathematical inconsistency. Appendix B.4 defines the purported negative-entropy reward as minus the sum of p log p, which is positive entropy. Maximizing the written reward therefore encourages entropy rather than minimizing it. This could be a transcription error, but without clarification the central comparison supporting superiority over entropy minimization cannot be trusted.

Training specifications materially conflict. Section 4 gives a MATH learning rate of 3e-5 and KL coefficient 0.005, whereas Table 10 lists 3e-6 and 0.0005. The Codeforces learning rate also differs by tenfold, and Appendix B.2 specifies sixteen completions while Table 10 gives fourteen. These discrepancies are especially consequential because the paper documents strong sensitivity to these settings.

The evaluation does not adequately separate reasoning improvements from prompt and output-format adaptation. The Qwen2.5-1.5B base model essentially fails under the chosen chat template, and many qualitative gains involve replacing placeholders or malformed responses. Base-appropriate prompting, format-adaptation controls, and length-controlled reasoning comparisons are needed. Results on instruction-tuned models partly address this concern but do not resolve it.

No repeated-training-seed results or uncertainty estimates are reported. Several comparisons are small, and the headline claim of matching GRPO conceals consistent deficits on the main small-model math results. Transfer advantages are also heterogeneous: OLMo's CRUXEval performance decreases, and Qwen3-14B does not improve on LiveCodeBench.

The claim that online self-certainty prevents reward exploitation exceeds the evidence. Short training runs and a particular frozen-scorer failure demonstrate relative stability in those settings, not general protection. Appendix B.10 itself reports collapse under changed learning rates, model initialization, and noisy data. Likewise, longer explanations and ten inspected code problems do not establish the proposed mechanism of improved understanding.

Novelty is narrower than the proposed new RLIF paradigm suggests: the method combines an existing confidence metric with standard GRPO, alongside acknowledged concurrent confidence and entropy-based approaches. A reliable, appropriately configured comparison with the closest methods is therefore crucial. The current baseline ambiguity, reproducibility inconsistencies, and limited causal evidence leave the contribution below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The method is simple and practically relevant: replacing GRPO’s correctness reward with self-certainty enables post-training without gold answers or execution-based rewards.

The empirical coverage is substantial, including multiple model families, models up to 14B parameters, mathematical reasoning, code tasks, and instruction following. Table 4 provides meaningful positive evidence: Qwen2.5-14B reaches 77.0% on MATH500 versus 75.8% for GRPO.
The Qwen2.5-3B transfer results are promising: INTUITOR achieves 15.3% on LiveCodeBench and 41.6% on CRUXEval-O, compared with 8.5% and 34.1% for GRPO.
The appendix includes useful ablations on regularization, rollout size, alternative rewards, direct optimization, and online versus frozen reward scoring, alongside explicit failure cases.
weaknesses: The entropy baseline has a consequential specification error. Appendix B.4 defines its purported negative-entropy reward as minus the sum of p log p, which is positive entropy. Maximizing the stated reward encourages entropy maximization. This may be a typographical error, but until the implementation is verified, the comparison supporting self-certainty’s superiority over entropy minimization remains unresolved. Comparisons with appropriately tuned contemporary label-free methods are also insufficient.

Training specifications conflict materially. Section 4 gives learning rates of 3e-5 for MATH and 1e-5 for Codeforces, whereas Table 10 gives 3e-6 and 1e-6. The default small-model KL coefficient is 0.005 in the main text but 0.0005 in Table 10; Appendix B.2 specifies 16 rollouts for larger models while Table 10 specifies 14. These discrepancies are especially serious because the paper documents strong sensitivity to these settings.

The headline reasoning gains are partly confounded by prompt adaptation. Qwen2.5-1.5B starts at 0.2% GSM8K accuracy under an unfamiliar chat template, and the paper explicitly describes learning to eliminate gibberish and follow that template. Base-compatible prompting and controls that isolate formatting improvements are needed to establish how much improvement reflects reasoning. Results on stronger and instruction-tuned models help, but do not resolve this attribution.

The claims of matching supervised RL and superior transfer need qualification. In Table 1, INTUITOR trails GRPO on both mathematical benchmarks at both model sizes. Transfer advantages vary across models: OLMo shows essentially equal LiveCodeBench performance and declining CRUXEval accuracy, while Qwen3-14B does not improve on LiveCodeBench. No repeated-seed results or uncertainty intervals establish the reliability of smaller differences.

The novelty is narrower than the proposed new RLIF paradigm suggests: the method combines an existing confidence statistic with standard GRPO, while several acknowledged works already optimize intrinsic confidence or entropy without labels. The proposed explanation through improved understanding and structured reasoning remains speculative. Longer outputs and qualitative categorization of ten questions do not establish a causal mechanism or distinguish useful reasoning from verbosity.

The assertion that online self-certainty prevents reward exploitation exceeds the evidence. Figure 7 demonstrates stability in one finite experimental setting, while Appendix B.10 reports collapse under other learning rates, models, and data conditions. Figure 8 establishes confidence–correctness association, not calibration or immunity to reward hacking. Together with the unresolved baseline and reproducibility issues, these limitations leave the submission below the acceptance threshold despite promising empirical findings.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: improving LLM performance without answer labels or executable verifiers. Using self-certainty as a GRPO reward is simple and potentially useful across domains.

The empirical evidence extends beyond the small models highlighted in the main text. On Qwen2.5-14B, INTUITOR achieves 77.0% MATH500 accuracy versus 75.8% for GRPO, and 56.0% CRUXEval-O accuracy versus 52.0%. Experiments also include Qwen3, Llama, and OLMo.
Math-to-code transfer is promising: Qwen2.5-3B improves from 9.3% to 15.3% on LiveCodeBench, compared with 8.5% after GRPO training.

The appendix provides substantial investigation of KL regularization, reward alternatives, direct optimization, rollout size, and failure cases. The online-versus-frozen reward comparison is particularly informative.
weaknesses: The central entropy-minimization comparison has an unresolved sign error. Appendix B.4 defines its reward as minus the average sum of p log p, which is positive entropy; maximizing this reward encourages entropy maximization. This could be a typographical error, but the implementation must be clarified before the reported failures establish superiority over negative-entropy rewards.

Training specifications materially conflict. Section 4 gives learning rates of 3e-5 for math and 1e-5 for code, while Table 10 gives 3e-6 and 1e-6. The default small-model KL coefficient is 0.005 in the text but 0.0005 in Table 10; Appendix B.2 specifies 16 rollouts while Table 10 specifies 14. These differences hinder reproduction and interpretation of stability comparisons.

Novelty is narrower than the claimed introduction of a new RL paradigm. Self-certainty and GRPO are existing components, and the paper acknowledges closely related confidence-based and entropy-based self-improvement methods. Its strongest contribution is empirical validation of this particular reward, making reliable comparisons with those alternatives especially important.

No repeated training runs or uncertainty estimates are reported. Generalization advantages are also mixed: INTUITOR trails GRPO on small-model math results, Qwen2.5-1.5B CRUXEval, and Qwen2.5-7B LiveCodeBench; OLMo's CRUXEval performance decreases after training. The evidence supports useful improvements, but not uniformly superior transfer.

Claims that online self-certainty prevents reward exploitation exceed the evidence from short training runs. Appendix B.10 itself reports collapse under different learning rates or unsuitable data. The results demonstrate conditional stability rather than a general safeguard.

The reasoning interpretation remains insufficiently isolated from formatting and response-length changes. The Qwen2.5-1.5B baseline performs poorly under the chat template, prompts explicitly request step-by-step reasoning, and the behavioral analysis uses only ten questions. Native-template baselines and length-controlled comparisons would better establish improved reasoning beyond instruction adaptation.
